title: Toss It High
blurb: Add the yusheng ingredients in order as each phrase is called, then toss it high.
fact: Yusheng plays on sounds: 鱼 (fish) sounds like 余 (abundance), and 生 means both ‘raw’ and ‘life’. So the name itself wishes you abundance and long life.
credit: Source: Lohei, Our Way: Celebrating Togetherness, Tossing Up Abundance and Yusheng and Lo Hei (ICH-096), Roots.sg, National Heritage Board. Ingredient illustrations are original AI-generated artwork. Phrase audio is computer-generated; the "Huat ah!" recording is from djbeng.com.

opening.saying: 恭喜发财 · 万事如意
opening.pinyin: Gong xi fa cai · Wan shi ru yi
opening.wish: Congratulations for your great wealth! May all your wishes be fulfilled!

ingredients.name: Raw fish
ingredients.wish: May you have abundance every year!
ingredients.note: ‘Fish’ (yu) and ‘abundance’ (yu) sound the same in Mandarin. Early immigrants swapped carp for wolf herring to avoid parasites.

ingredients.name: Pomelo or lime
ingredients.wish: May you have great luck and prosperity!
ingredients.note: Yusheng was brought to Singapore by Cantonese and Teochew immigrants from China.

ingredients.name: Spices
ingredients.wish: May you attract wealth and treasures!
ingredients.note: The first chefs paired five-spice powder or pepper with 五福临门: five blessings of longevity, wealth, health, kindness and peace.

ingredients.name: Oil and plum sauce
ingredients.wish: May your capital bring you ten-thousand-fold profits!
ingredients.saying: 一本万利 · 财源广进
ingredients.pinyin: Yi ben wan li · Cai yuan guang jin
ingredients.note: In the 1900s, yusheng was just raw fish, cucumber, radish and coriander, topped with vinegar, oil and sugar.

ingredients.name: Shredded carrot
ingredients.note: ‘Red’ (hong), for the carrot's colour, sounds like ‘great’ (hong). The chefs first paired this phrase with red pickled ginger.

ingredients.name: Green radish
ingredients.note: ‘Green’ (qing) is the same qing as in qing chun, ‘youthful’.

ingredients.name: White radish
ingredients.wish: May you progress quickly and rise to greater heights!
ingredients.saying: 风生水起 · 步步高升
ingredients.pinyin: Feng sheng shui qi · Bu bu gao sheng
ingredients.note: In 1964, four chefs at Lai Wah Restaurant, the ‘Four Heavenly Kings’, created the seven-coloured yusheng, 七彩鱼生.

ingredients.name: Crushed peanuts
ingredients.wish: May your house be filled with gold and silver!
ingredients.note: The Four Heavenly Kings' version added peanuts and flour crisps for more fragrance and texture.

ingredients.name: Sesame seeds
ingredients.note: Yusheng caught on when the four chefs added it to their Chinese New Year set dinners, and took off with younger diners in the 1970s.

ingredients.name: Golden flour crisps
ingredients.wish: May your floor be covered in gold!
ingredients.note: The deep-fried crisps are shaped like golden pillows.

content.tossPrompt: Everyone stands, chopsticks in hand. Flick up from the plate: the higher the toss, the better your fortune for the year.

figures.alt: Diners toss a plate of yusheng together with chopsticks
figures.caption: Lo hei and eating yusheng have become a tradition of Chinese New Year in Singapore. Photo: Yusheng and Lo Hei (ICH-096), Roots.sg.

figures.alt: A colourful plate of yusheng as a table centrepiece
figures.caption: Yusheng is usually the first dish at any family or company gathering during Chinese New Year. Photo: National Heritage Board, from Lohei, Our Way, Roots.sg.

figures.alt: Slices of raw fish for yusheng
figures.caption: The fish is usually salmon or wolf herring. In recent years abalone and tuna have appeared too. Photo: National Heritage Board, from Lohei, Our Way, Roots.sg.
Master chef Hooi Kok Wai, one of the ‘Four Heavenly Kings’, still spends most of his day at wet markets looking for fresh fish. Photo: National Heritage Board, from Lohei, Our Way, Roots.sg.

cards.title: More than 2,000 years
cards.text: The earliest written record of eating raw fish in China dates to 823 BCE. Fishermen in Jiangmen and Shunde, in Guangdong, feasted on raw carp on Renri (人日), the seventh day of the Lunar New Year, believed to be the birthday of all humanity.

cards.title: A name of abundance
cards.text: 鱼 (fish) sounds like 余 (abundance), and 生 means both ‘raw’ and ‘life’, so yusheng wishes for abundance and long life. Cantonese and Teochew immigrants brought the dish to Singapore.

cards.title: The Four Heavenly Kings
cards.text: Loong Yik Kee Restaurant sold its own version in 1933. In 1964 four chefs at Lai Wah Restaurant created the seven-coloured 七彩鱼生, adding peanuts and flour crisps, and put it on their Chinese New Year set menus. It took off in the 1970s.

cards.title: Why everyone stands
cards.text: The chefs paired phrases with some ingredients, and diners made up the rest. The dish was big and hard to mix, so diners may have stood up to help the waiter, and standing became a celebration of togetherness. The higher the toss, the better the year ahead.

cards.title: Lo hei today
cards.text: There are halal, vegetarian and vegan versions (with gluten strips in place of fish), takeaway and supermarket packs. Friends and colleagues from every culture join in.
